To undulate means to move in a smooth, continuous, wave-like motion — gently rising and falling, or curving in and out, over and over again in a flowing rhythm. Think of the surface of the ocean. It doesn't crash violently at every point; instead, it swells up, dips down, swells up again, dips down again — endlessly, smoothly, rhythmically. That graceful, rolling, wave-like movement is exactly what "undulate" describes.

The single most important thing to lock in your mind: undulating motion is always smooth, always rhythmic, and always wave-like. It is never sharp, sudden, or jerky.
The two main ways it's used

"Undulate" works in two closely related ways — to describe movement, and to describe the shape of something.

1. Movement — This is the most common use. Something undulates when it moves in flowing waves, either through space or within itself.

A snake undulates across the floor — its body forms a series of smooth S-curves that ripple from its head all the way down to its tail, propelling it forward. A flag undulates in the breeze — the fabric rises and falls in smooth, traveling waves from the pole to the tip. The surface of a lake undulates when the wind brushes across it. A belly dancer undulates her torso — her body flows in a continuous, controlled wave-like motion. In every one of these cases, the motion is fluid, not choppy.

2. Shape or appearance — Sometimes "undulate" describes not active movement, but the wave-like form of something, especially a landscape or surface.

Rolling hills undulate across the countryside — they rise and fall in gentle curves, one after another, like a frozen wave. A road that winds through such terrain can be said to undulate. Here, the word captures the visual impression of something that looks wave-shaped even when it isn't actively moving.

A crucial nuance: what makes undulation different from just "moving up and down"

Not every up-and-down motion counts as undulating. A piston in a car engine shoots up and down rapidly and mechanically — that is not undulation. A person jumping on a trampoline goes up and down — still not undulation. What separates undulation from those is smoothness, continuity, and a wave-like quality that travels through the thing itself or across its surface. The motion flows; it doesn't bounce or snap.

Also notice that undulation isn't always perfectly vertical (up and down). It can be horizontal, diagonal, or flowing in any direction — as long as the motion is wave-like and smooth. A ribbon trailing in the wind undulates side to side. Sound waves can metaphorically undulate — rising and falling in pitch or volume in a smooth, rhythmic way.

"Undulate" can work with or without a direct object.

Most of the time it is used without a direct object (intransitive): "The grass undulated in the wind." Here, the grass itself is doing the undulating.

Sometimes it is used with a direct object (transitive): "The dancer undulated her arms." Here, a person is making something else move in a wave-like way. This use is less common but perfectly correct.

Undulation is often described in terms of how pronounced or gentle it is. A field of wheat might undulate softly or gently. The sea might undulate wildly in a storm. Even in a storm, though, the word still implies that underlying wave-like rhythm — just amplified.

You'll encounter "undulate" frequently in writing about nature (water, land, plants in the wind), the human body (in dance, movement, or anatomy), and occasionally in abstract or figurative contexts (music, light, emotion described poetically as undulating).
The word family you'll meet alongside it

Since you'll encounter these constantly once you know "undulate," it helps to know them:

Undulating is the adjective or present participle form. "The undulating hills stretched to the horizon." "The snake's undulating body moved silently through the grass." This is arguably the most common form you'll see in writing.

Undulation is the noun — it refers to a single wave-like movement or the quality of being wave-like. "The gentle undulation of the water was calming." "The undulations of the terrain made driving difficult."

Undulatory is a formal adjective meaning "of or relating to undulation" — used mostly in scientific writing (undulatory motion, undulatory waves).
One sentence to remember it by

If you ever need to recall what "undulate" means, picture this: a long silk ribbon trailing out the window of a moving car, rippling and waving in the air behind it. That flowing, smooth, continuous, wave-like movement — that is undulation.
